[AKHFASH:v2p580/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Mā in wa-nafsin wa-mā sawwāhā means the One who fashioned it; God swears by Himself as Lord of the soul He formed, and the oath's answer is qad aflaḥa man zakkāhā.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p205/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | God swears by the soul and its fashioning, then teaches it to recognize righteous and wicked deeds, a knowledge shared by ignorant and learned alike.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p285/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | ما and من share an origin: من is used for people, while ما is used for nonhuman things.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p285/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda takes ما in these passages, including «ونفس وما سواها», to mean من, “who.” | mentions 92:3, 91:6
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p285/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr says ما means “that which”; Meccans use the same relative pronoun in their saying when they hear thunder.
[TAB:91:7/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God is the one who fashioned the soul, created it, and proportioned its creation; here mā is used in place of man, ‘who.’
[TAB:91:7/r2] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Alternatively, mā with what follows can be a verbal noun: the oath is by the soul and its fashioning.
[IBNABIHATIM:v10p3436#3/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says people's deeds are already decreed, yet they work because each person is prepared for the destination for which God created him; he cites the soul and its inspiration toward wickedness and piety.
[NAHHAS:v5p235/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Sawwāhā means its proportioning; interpreting mā as ‘the one who proportioned it’ would refer to God and require man, not mā.
[THALABI:v10p212#3/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | God proportioned the soul's creation and inspired it with both wickedness and reverence.
[THALABI:v10p212#3/r17] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو الأسود الدؤلي عن عمران بن حصين | reports | Imran asks whether people's actions are predetermined or arise from prophetic instruction and proof. Abu al-Aswad answers that all is decreed, adding that God created and owns everything and is not questioned while people are. | mentions 21:23
[THALABI:v10p213/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | God creates each person for one of two final destinations and prepares that person for it, as the following verses affirm. | mentions 91:7, 91:8
[MAWARDI:91:7/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الحسن | reports | The soul is Adam, and the one who fashioned him is God.
[MAWARDI:91:7/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | reports | Another view takes the soul to mean every soul.
[MAWARDI:91:7/r3] MAWARDI, d. 450 · ابن جريج | reports | On the universal reading, God made souls equal in health and equal in punishment.
[MAWARDI:91:7/r4] MAWARDI, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | On the universal reading, God formed each soul and proportioned its creation.
[MAWARDI:91:7/r5] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | A further possibility is that God fashioned the soul with reason, which gives it distinction over all animals.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p282/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another view understands the soul as every soul.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p282/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن جريج | reports | On the universal-soul view, God made people equal in health and equal in punishment.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p282/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | On the universal-soul view, God proportioned and balanced the soul's creation.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p282/r13] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A further possibility is that God endowed the soul with intellect, distinguishing it from all animals.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p282/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن | reports | One view identifies the soul as Adam and its fashioner as God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p54/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | “What fashioned it” means the One who created and proportioned the soul’s limbs.
[WAHIDI-QT:91:7/r1] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | The oath refers to the shaping of the soul's creation.
[JISHUMI:v10p7431/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The wāw in this sūra’s openings is the oath particle and puts following nouns in genitive; the oath particles are bāʾ, then its derivative wāw, then tāʾ, which only precedes God’s name.
[JISHUMI:v10p7431/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قتادة وأبي علي | reports | Qatāda and Abū ʿAlī explain the shaping of the soul as proportioning its creation, limbs, senses, and channels.
[JISHUMI:v10p7431/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan supplies “God” as the maker: God built the sky, spread the earth, and fashioned the soul.
[JISHUMI:v10p7431/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another construction takes the oath to be by the sky and its builder, the earth and its spreader, and the soul and its shaper.
[JISHUMI:v10p7431/r22] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو مسلم | reports | Abū Muslim connects the fāʾ of “inspired it” to “the soul and what shaped it,” meaning God shaped the soul and then inspired it.
[BAGHAWI:91:7/r1] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | God proportioned the soul's creation and made its limbs even.
[BAGHAWI:91:7/r2] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · عطاء | reports | ʿAta takes “a soul” to mean all that God created of jinn and humans.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p438/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | God proportioned the soul’s creation and its limbs; Ata says ‘soul’ here means all that God created of jinn and humans.
[KASHSHAF:91:5/r1] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | prefers | The particle ma should be relative rather than a verbal noun: the latter weakens the sequence into fa-alhamaha; ma also conveys an adjectival meaning such as the mighty builder and wise shaper.
[KASHSHAF:91:6/r1] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | prefers | The particle ma should be relative rather than a verbal noun: the latter weakens the sequence into fa-alhamaha; ma also conveys an adjectival meaning such as the mighty builder and wise shaper.
[KASHSHAF:91:7/r1] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | reports | The indefinite soul may be one particular soul, Adam's, or may mean every soul, with the indefinite form magnifying and multiplying its scope.
[KASHSHAF:91:7/r2] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | reports | The second reading takes it as every soul, like the cited indefinite expression. | mentions 81:14
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The repeated wāws can govern both accusative and genitive: the oath-wāw omits its verb altogether and substitutes for it, while coordinated wāws inherit that double function, resolving the apparent two-governor problem.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | prefers | In وما بناها, وما طحاها, and وما سواها, ما is best taken as a relative pronoun, not a verbal noun, which would spoil the sequence; it means the mighty Creator who built and fashioned them.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The indefinite نفس may denote Adam specifically, or all souls, left indefinite to convey abundance as in another verse. | mentions 81:14
[IBNATIYYA:91:7/r1] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The sworn-by soul is a generic noun; its fashioning perfects its intellect and reflection, which the following verse's fāʾ links to inspiration. | mentions 91:8
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p488/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The sworn-by soul is the human genus; its being fashioned means completing its intellect and discernment, as the following clause explains.
[TABRISI:91:1-15/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · عطاء | reports | The soul may mean all that God created among jinn and humans; al-Hasan instead takes it as Adam and the one who formed him.
[TABRISI:91:1-15/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | God fashioned the soul's form and balanced its limbs; another view says intellect distinguishes people from other animals.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p566/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | reports | Mā can mean “who” or “the one that” in oaths; some group it with the relative sense.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p566/r7] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أبو عمرو | reports | Ibn Qutayba reports Abū ʿAmr’s view that mā in the oaths means “that which.”
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p566/r8] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل مكة | reports | Meccans say on hearing thunder, “Glory to the One whom it glorifies,” illustrating mā as a relative form.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#3/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن ومجاهد وأبو عبيدة | reports | One view takes mā as “who”: “and who built it”; some instead read it as the relative pronoun “that which.” The same two analyses apply to 91:6 and 91:7. | mentions 91:6, 91:7
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#3/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · قتادة والزجاج | reports | A second view makes mā a verbal noun: “and its building”; this also applies to 91:6 and 91:7. | mentions 91:6, 91:7
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#3/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو عمران الجوني | reports | Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī and others read man instead of mā in all three phrases, “who built/spread/fashioned them.” | mentions 91:6, 91:7
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#3/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن | reports | One view says the soul is Adam.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#3/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عطاء | reports | A second view says it means all souls.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138#3/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The meaning of fashioning the soul was discussed at 82:7. | mentions 82:7
[RAZI:91:7/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | If nafs means the body, its fashioning is the proportioning of its limbs, as anatomy shows.
[RAZI:91:7/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | If nafs means the governing faculty, its fashioning is by giving it powers of hearing, sight, imagination, thought, and memory, as psychology shows.
[RAZI:91:7/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | One explanation of the indefinite noun is that it singles out the prophetic, sanctified soul as chief over the world of composite beings.
[RAZI:91:7/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | This view reasons that every multiplicity has

a chief: composites are headed by animals, animal kinds by humans, human kinds by prophets, and the prophets by one supreme leader.
[RAZI:91:7/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | Alternatively, the indefinite noun means every soul and conveys abundance, as in “each soul shall know what it has brought.” | mentions 81:14
[RAZI:91:7/r6] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | Souls belong to innumerable animal kinds; each is distinct in its defining qualities, and human understanding cannot grasp even the few qualities of fleas and mosquitoes, much less God’s secrets. | mentions 16:8
[RAZI-FULL:v1p72/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Razi presents an affinity principle: pure, luminous human souls join pure spirits that aid virtue, while corrupt, dark souls join evil spirits that aid sin and aggression.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p72/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفريق الثالث | reports | The third group denies lower spirits but affirms separate celestial spirits, which it describes as high, powerful, and differing in their essences and natures.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p72/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفريق الثالث | reports | This group analogizes each celestial soul's assigned sphere to a human soul's body: each first attaches to its heart or planet, then its influence spreads through the whole body or sphere and world.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p72/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفريق الثالث | reports | As subtle spirits from heart and brain travel through arteries and nerves to distribute life, sensation, and motion throughout the body, planetary radial rays carry planetary influence to every region of the world.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p72/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفريق الثالث | reports | The bodily faculties of nutrition, growth, generation, and sensation are outcomes of the governing soul; similarly planetary rays generate particular human souls, such as Zayd and ʿAmr, as offspring of planetary souls.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p72/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفريق الثالث | reports | Since planetary souls differ in essence, souls associated with Saturn form a mutually homogeneous group marked by affection, while differing in nature from souls associated with Jupiter.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The sura urges obedience and warns against disobedience; oaths by beneficial created things prompt reflection and gratitude because divine oaths weigh heavily on the heart.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p173#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi accepts the concern that an infinitival mā disrupts the sequence and the Qadi's concern about delaying an oath by the sky's Creator; he answers that the order stages sense before reason.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p173#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After the sun's four attributes, God is described through three acts over the sky, earth, and composite beings, represented by the soul; this guides reason from sensible creation to divine majesty.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p174#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If nafs means the body, its proportioning is the balanced arrangement of its organs; if it means the governing faculty, God gave it hearing, sight, imagination, thought, and memory.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p174#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One reading of the indefinite 'a soul' is the unique sacred prophetic soul, chief among composites, animals, humans, and prophets.
[RAZI-FULL:v31p174#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Alternatively it means every soul; the indefinite signals multiplicity, since every animal species has a distinct soul and properties beyond human comprehension. | mentions 81:14, 16:8
[RAZI-FULL:v31p174/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God's three signs cover the physical world: simple bodies include upper heaven and lower earth, while the noblest composites are ensouled beings; the unseen is inferred from the visible.
[QURTUBI:91:7/r1] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قيل | reports | One parsing takes mā as a verbal noun, so the phrase means the soul and its fashioning.
[QURTUBI:91:7/r2] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another parsing takes mā as meaning who, referring to God as the one who fashioned the soul.
[QURTUBI:91:7/r3] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قيل | reports | The soul may refer either to Adam or to every human soul.

[QURTUBI:91:7/r7] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | God swears by His creation because its wondrous workmanship points to Him.

[QURTUBI-FULL:91:7/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Sawa means to prepare; Mujahid glosses it as forming the soul’s creation and proportioning it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:91:7/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The preceding nouns are genitive as objects of the oath; God swears by created signs and their wonders.

[BAYDAWI:91:7/r2] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | The indefinite “soul” may indicate abundance, as in the verse “a soul will know what it brought,” or may magnify it; the referent is Adam's soul. | mentions 81:14

[BAYDAWI-FULL:91:5-8/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The indefinite soul may generalize across souls, as at 81:14, or magnify and refer specifically to Adam. | mentions 81:14

[NASAFI-FULL:v4p342/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | The preferred analysis makes ma relative, describing the mighty Creator who built the sky and the wise One who fashioned the soul; the soul is singled out as Adam's or left indefinite to signify all souls or abundance.
[QASHANI:91:8/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The soul may mean the animal potency impressed in animal spirit, the whole composite, or the rational soul; God balanced it between lordship and lowliness, neither bodily darkness nor spiritual light.

[BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r15] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The oath’s implied conclusion is that God gave souls differing dispositions and capacity for purification or corruption, urging people to purify themselves in view of resurrection.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p438/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The outward cosmos has an inward human counterpart, so celestial and terrestrial features can be read as faculties and bodily processes.
